label: Phaedo · The True Earth and the Death
title: The True Earth and the Death
paragraphs: But this much, gentlemen, he said, it is right to keep in mind: if the soul is immortal, then it needs care, not only for the sake of this time that we call living, but for the sake of all time, and now the risk would indeed seem terrible, if anyone is going to neglect it. For if death were a riddance of everything, it would be a windfall for the wicked when they die, to be rid at once of the body and of their own wickedness along with the soul. But as it is, since the soul is plainly immortal, there can be no other escape from evils for it, and no safety, except to become as good and as wise as possible. For the soul comes to Hades with nothing else but its education and upbringing, and these are the very things that are said to do the greatest good or the greatest harm to the dead man, right at the start of his journey there.

What is said is this. When each person has died, each one's guardian spirit, the one that had been allotted to him in life, sets out to lead him to a certain place. There those who have been gathered must submit to judgment and then make the journey to Hades with that guide who has been assigned to bring those from here over there. And when they have met there with what they must meet with, and stayed for the time they must, another guide brings them back here again, after many long cycles of time.

Now the journey is not as Aeschylus' Telephus says. He says that a simple path leads to Hades, but to me it seems to be neither simple nor single. For then there would be no need of guides; no one, surely, would go wrong in any direction if there were only one road. But as it is, it seems to have many forks and places where three roads meet. I say this judging by the sacrifices and the customs here. Now the orderly and wise soul follows, and is not ignorant of what is around it. But the soul that is full of desire for the body, as I said before, after fluttering around it and around the visible region for a long time, after much resistance and much suffering, is led away by force and with difficulty by the guardian spirit assigned to it. And when it arrives where the others are, the soul that is impure and has done something of that sort, that has laid its hand to unjust killings or committed other such acts, which are akin to these and the work of kindred souls — this soul everyone flees and turns away from, and no one is willing to be its fellow traveler or its guide. It wanders by itself, held in utter helplessness, until certain lengths of time have passed; and when they have come, it is carried by necessity to the dwelling that suits it. But the soul that has passed through life purely and with measure finds gods for fellow travelers and guides, and each such soul comes to dwell in the place that is proper to it.
And the earth has many wonderful regions, and it is itself neither of the kind nor of the size that it is believed to be by those who usually talk about the earth, as someone has convinced me.
What do you mean by that, Socrates? said Simmias. I too have heard a great deal about the earth, you know, but not these things that convince you. So I would gladly hear them.

Well, Simmias, I do not think it takes the skill of Glaucus to describe what they are. But to show that they are true seems to me too hard for the skill of Glaucus. For one thing, I might not even be able to do it; and for another, even if I knew how, my life, Simmias, seems to me not long enough for the length of the argument. Still, nothing prevents me from telling what I am convinced the form of the earth is, and its regions.
Why, said Simmias, even that is enough.

I am convinced, then, he said, first, that if the earth is in the middle of the sky and is round, it has no need of air to keep it from falling, nor of any other such constraint. The likeness of the sky itself to itself in every direction, and the even balance of the earth itself, are enough to hold it. For a thing evenly balanced, set in the middle of something alike all around, will have no cause to lean more or less in any direction, but being the same on every side it will stay where it is without leaning. This, then, he said, is the first thing I am convinced of.
And rightly so, said Simmias.

Next, he said, that it is something very large, and that we who live between Phasis and the Pillars of Heracles live in a small part of it, around the sea, like ants or frogs around a marsh, and that many other people live elsewhere in many such places. For everywhere around the earth there are many hollows, of every kind in shape and in size, into which the water and the mist and the air have flowed together. But the earth itself lies pure in the pure sky, where the stars are, the sky that most of those who usually talk about such things call ether. The water and mist and air are the dregs of this, and they are always flowing together into the hollows of the earth.

So we, living in its hollows, do not know it, and think we are living up on top of the earth. It is as if someone living in the middle of the floor of the ocean thought he was living on top of the sea, and, seeing the sun and the other stars through the water, took the sea to be the sky; and because of his slowness and weakness had never once reached the top of the sea, nor seen, by coming out and lifting his head from the sea into this region here, how much purer and more beautiful it is than their own, nor heard of it from anyone else who had seen. That is the very thing that has happened to us too. For living in a hollow of the earth, we think we live on top of it, and we call the air sky, as if this were the sky and the stars moved through it. But it is the same thing: through weakness and slowness we are not able to make our way out to the last edge of the air. For if anyone should come to the top of it, or grow wings and fly up, he would lift his head and see — just as fish here lift their heads out of the sea and see the things here, so he would see the things there. And if his nature were strong enough to bear the sight, he would know that that is the true sky and the true light and the earth that is truly earth.

For this earth here, and the stones, and the whole region here, are spoiled and eaten away, as things in the sea are by the brine. Nothing worth speaking of grows in the sea, and nothing there, so to speak, is perfect. There are hollow rocks and sand and mud beyond measure and mire, wherever there is earth as well, and they are not in any way fit to be judged beside the beautiful things among us. And those things there, in their turn, would be seen to surpass the things among us by much more still. For if it is also a fine thing to tell a story, Simmias, it is worth hearing what the things on the earth under the sky are really like.
Why, Socrates, said Simmias, we for our part would gladly hear this story.

Well then, my friend, he said, it is said, first, that the earth itself, if one looked at it from above, is to the eye like those balls made of twelve pieces of leather: many-colored, marked off in colors, of which the colors here, the ones the painters use, are like samples. There the whole earth is made of such colors, and of colors much brighter and purer than these. One part is purple and wonderful in its beauty, another is like gold, and the part that is white is whiter than chalk or snow; and it is made up of the other colors in the same way, and of still more colors, and more beautiful ones, than any we have seen. For even these hollows of the earth, being full of water and air, present a kind of color as they glisten among the variety of the other colors, so that the earth appears as one continuous many-colored form.

And on this earth, being such as it is, the things that grow grow in proportion: trees and flowers and fruits. And the mountains too, in the same way, and the stones, have in the same proportion a smoothness and a transparency and colors that are more beautiful. The little stones here, these that are prized, are fragments of them: carnelians and jaspers and emeralds and all such things. But there, there is nothing that is not of that kind, and more beautiful still than these. And the cause of this is that those stones are pure, and not eaten away or spoiled as the ones here are by rot and brine, by the things that have flowed together here, which bring ugliness and disease to stones and earth, and to animals and plants besides. And the earth itself is adorned with all these, and with gold and silver too, and the other things of that kind. For they lie there in plain sight, many in number and large and everywhere on the earth, so that to see it is a sight for happy spectators.

And there are living creatures on it, many others and human beings too, some living inland, some around the air as we live around the sea, and some on islands that the air flows around, lying close to the mainland. In a word, what water and the sea are to us for our use, the air is there; and what air is to us, the ether is to them. Their seasons are so tempered that they are free of disease and live a much longer time than the people here, and in sight and hearing and wisdom and all such things they stand as far from us as air stands from water, and ether from air, in purity. And they also have groves and temples of the gods, in which gods really do dwell; and utterances and prophecies and perceptions of the gods, and meetings of that kind, come to them face to face. And the sun and moon and stars are seen by them as they really are, and the rest of their happiness is in keeping with this.

Such, then, is the nature of the earth as a whole, and of the things around the earth. But within it, in its hollows, there are many regions in a circle around the whole: some deeper and more open than the one we live in; some deeper, but with a narrower opening than our region; and some shallower in depth than the one here, and broader. All of these are joined to one another under the earth by passages bored in many places, some narrower and some wider, and they have ways through. By these much water flows from one into another, as into mixing bowls; and there are ever-flowing rivers of enormous size under the earth, of hot waters and of cold, and much fire and great rivers of fire, and many rivers of wet mud, some purer and some filthier, like the rivers of mud that flow in Sicily before the lava, and the lava itself. And each of the regions is filled with these, as the flow comes around to each of them at each time. And all these are moved up and down by a kind of swinging that is in the earth. And this swinging comes about through a nature of this sort.

One of the chasms of the earth is not only the largest but is also bored right through the whole earth. It is the one Homer spoke of when he said of it ‘very far off, where the deepest pit is under the earth,’ and which elsewhere both he and many other poets have called Tartarus. For into this chasm all the rivers flow together, and out of it they flow again; and each of them becomes such as the earth it flows through. And the cause of all the streams flowing out of here and flowing in is that this liquid has no bottom and no footing. So it swings and surges up and down, and the air and the breath around it do the same. For they follow along with it, both when it rushes toward the far side of the earth and when it rushes toward this side; and just as in those who breathe the breath is always flowing, breathed out and breathed in, so there too the breath, swinging along with the liquid, makes terrible and overwhelming winds as it goes in and as it goes out.

So when the water draws back into the region that is called below, it flows into the streams in that part of the earth and fills them, as people do who pump water in. And when again it leaves there and rushes this way, it fills the streams here once more; and these, when they have been filled, flow through the channels and through the earth, and each arriving at the places to which a way has been made for it, they make seas and lakes and rivers and springs. From there they sink under the earth again, some going around longer and more numerous regions, others fewer and shorter ones, and fall into Tartarus again, some far lower than where they were pumped out, others only a little. But all of them flow in below their outflow. Some flow in opposite the place where they poured out, and some on the same side. And there are some that go all the way around in a circle, coiling around the earth once or even several times like snakes, go down as low as they can and fall in again. It is possible to go down on either side as far as the middle, but no farther; for to both streams the part on either side is uphill.

Now there are many other streams, large and of every kind. But among these many there happen to be four in particular. The greatest of them, flowing outermost in a circle, is the one called Oceanus. Opposite it, and flowing the contrary way, is Acheron, which flows through other deserted regions and also under the earth, and arrives at the Acherusian lake. There the souls of most of the dead arrive, and after staying for certain appointed times, some longer, some shorter, they are sent out again to be born as living creatures.

The third river comes out between these two, and near its outlet it falls into a great region burning with much fire, and makes a lake larger than our sea, boiling with water and mud. From there it moves in a circle, turbid and muddy, and coiling around the earth it comes, among other places, to the edge of the Acherusian lake, without mixing with its water. And after coiling many times under the earth it falls into Tartarus at a lower point. This is the one they name Pyriphlegethon, and the lava streams blow up fragments of it wherever on the earth they happen to break out.

Opposite this one in turn the fourth river comes out, first into a region terrible and wild, as it is said, with a color all over like lapis lazuli, which they name the Stygian region; and the lake which the river makes by flowing in they name Styx. After falling in there and taking on terrible powers in its water, it sinks under the earth and, coiling, moves the contrary way to Pyriphlegethon and meets it at the Acherusian lake from the opposite side. And this river's water does not mix with any other either, but this one too goes around in a circle and falls into Tartarus opposite Pyriphlegethon. Its name, as the poets say, is Cocytus.

Such being the nature of these things, when the dead arrive at the place to which the guardian spirit brings each one, first they submit to judgment, both those who have lived well and piously and those who have not. And those who are found to have lived a middling life make their way to Acheron, board such vessels as there are for them, and on these arrive at the lake. There they dwell and are purified: by paying the penalty for their wrongs they are absolved, if anyone has done any wrong, and for their good deeds they win honors, each according to his worth. But those who are found to be incurable because of the greatness of their offenses, having committed many great robberies of temples, or many unjust and lawless killings, or whatever else is of that kind — these the lot that fits them hurls into Tartarus, and they never come out of it.

But those who are found to have committed offenses that are curable but great — who, for instance, did some violence to a father or a mother in anger and live the rest of their lives in regret, or who became killers in some other such way — these must fall into Tartarus; but when they have fallen in and been there a year, the wave throws them out, the killers by way of Cocytus, and those who struck a father or a mother by way of Pyriphlegethon. And when they are carried along and come to the Acherusian lake, there they shout and call, some to those they killed, others to those they abused; and having called them, they beg and plead with them to let them come out into the lake, and to receive them. If they persuade them, they come out and their evils end. If not, they are carried back into Tartarus and from there into the rivers again, and they do not stop suffering this until they persuade those they wronged. For this is the penalty laid on them by the judges.

But those who are found to have been outstanding in living piously — these are the ones who are freed and released from these regions in the earth as from prisons, and come up into the pure dwelling and make their home on top of the earth. And of these, those who have purified themselves enough by philosophy live altogether without bodies for all the time to come, and arrive at dwellings still more beautiful than these, which it is not easy to describe, nor is there time enough at present. But for the sake of these things that we have gone through, Simmias, one must do everything so as to share in virtue and wisdom in life. For the prize is fine and the hope is great.

Now to insist that these things are just as I have described them does not befit a man of sense. But that either this or something like it is true of our souls and their dwellings, since the soul is plainly immortal, this, it seems to me, is fitting, and worth the risk for one who thinks it is so — for the risk is a fine one — and one should chant such things to oneself like a spell, which is why I have been drawing out the story for so long. But for these reasons a man should be confident about his own soul, if in his life he has said goodbye to the other pleasures, those of the body, and to its ornaments, as foreign to him, judging that they do more harm than good, but has been in earnest about the pleasures of learning, and, having adorned his soul not with a foreign ornament but with its own, with self-command and justice and courage and freedom and truth, so awaits the journey to Hades.

You, then, Simmias and Cebes and the rest, he said, will each make the journey at some later time. But me now, already, as a man in a tragedy would say, fate is calling, and it is just about time for me to turn to the bath. For it seems better to bathe before drinking the poison, and not give the women the trouble of washing a corpse.

When he had said this, Crito said: Very well, Socrates. But what instructions do you leave with these men, or with me, about your children or about anything else? What could we do that would please you most?

What I always say, Crito, he said; nothing new. If you take care of your own selves, whatever you do will please me and mine and you yourselves, even if you promise nothing now. But if you neglect yourselves, and are not willing to live in the tracks, so to speak, of what we have said now and in the time before, then however much you promise at this moment, and however earnestly, you will do no good.
Then we will do our best to do as you say, he said. But in what way are we to bury you?

In any way you like, he said, if you can catch me, and I do not get away from you. And he laughed quietly, and looked toward us, and said: I cannot persuade Crito, gentlemen, that I am this Socrates here, the one who is talking with you now and setting each point of the argument in its place. He thinks I am that other one whom he will see in a little while as a corpse, and so he asks how he is to bury me. I have argued for a long time, and at length, that when I have drunk the poison I will stay with you no longer, but will go away to some happiness of the blessed; and all this, it seems, I have been saying to him for nothing, only to comfort you and to comfort myself. So stand surety for me to Crito, he said, with the opposite of the surety he gave the judges. He swore that I would stay. You must swear that I will not stay when I die, but will go away and be gone. Then Crito will bear it more easily, and when he sees my body being burned or buried he will not be distressed for me, as if I were suffering something terrible; and he will not say at the funeral that he is laying out Socrates, or carrying him to the grave, or burying him. For be sure of this, my good Crito, he said: to speak wrongly is not only a false note in itself; it also does some harm to the soul. No, you must be of good courage, and say that it is my body you are burying; and bury it in whatever way pleases you and you think most in keeping with custom.

When he had said this, he got up and went into another room to bathe. Crito followed him, and he told us to wait. So we waited, talking among ourselves about what had been said and going over it again, and then again speaking of how great a misfortune had come upon us; for we simply felt that we were losing a father, and would live the rest of our lives as orphans. When he had bathed, and his children had been brought to him — he had two small sons and one who was grown — and the women of his household had come, he talked with them in front of Crito and gave them the instructions he wished. Then he told the women and the children to go, and came back to us himself. By now it was near sunset, for he had spent a long time inside. He came and sat down, fresh from his bath, and after that he did not say much.

Then the officer of the Eleven came and stood beside him and said: Socrates, I will not have to blame you for what I blame in others, that they are angry with me and curse me when I give them the order to drink the poison, as the authorities require. You I have come to know in other ways too, during this time, as the noblest and gentlest and best man who has ever come here; and now especially I am sure that you are not angry with me, for you know who is responsible, but with them. So now — you know what I have come to tell you — farewell, and try to bear as easily as you can what must be. And with that he burst into tears, and turned, and went away.

Socrates looked up at him and said: Farewell to you too; and we will do as you say. And then to us he said: What a courteous man he is! All this time he has been coming in to me, and sometimes he would talk with me, and he was the best of men; and now how generously he weeps for me. But come, Crito, let us obey him. Let someone bring the poison, if it has been ground. If not, let the man grind it.

And Crito said: But I think, Socrates, that the sun is still on the mountains and has not yet set. And I know that others have drunk it very late, after the order was given them, when they had eaten and drunk their fill, and some had even been with those they happened to desire. Do not hurry. There is still time.

And Socrates said: It is reasonable, Crito, that the people you speak of do these things, for they think they gain by doing them. And it is reasonable that I will not do them. For I think I would gain nothing by drinking a little later, except to make myself a laughingstock in my own eyes, clinging to life and being sparing of it when there is nothing left. Come, he said, do as I ask, and do not refuse.

When Crito heard this, he nodded to the slave who was standing near. The slave went out, and after a long while he came back with the man who was to give the poison, who carried it ready ground in a cup. When Socrates saw the man he said: Well, my good man, you understand these things. What must I do?
Nothing, he said, but drink it and walk about until a heaviness comes into your legs, and then lie down. That way it will do its work. And with that he held out the cup to Socrates.

He took it, and quite cheerfully, Echecrates, without a tremor and without any change of color or of face, but looking up at the man from under his brows like a bull, as he used to do, he said: What do you say about pouring a libation to someone from this drink? Is it allowed or not?
We grind only as much, Socrates, he said, as we think is the right amount to drink.

I understand, he said. But I suppose one may pray to the gods, and one must, that the move from here to there may be a fortunate one. That is my prayer, and so may it be. And as he said this he put the cup to his lips, and quite readily and calmly he drank it off.

Until then most of us had been fairly well able to hold back our tears. But when we saw him drinking, and saw that he had drunk, we could do so no longer. In spite of myself my own tears came in a flood, so that I covered my face and wept for myself — not for him, no, but for my own fortune, in losing such a man as my friend. Crito had got up and gone out even before I did, because he could not hold back his tears. And Apollodorus, who even before this had never stopped weeping, now broke out roaring, weeping and distressed, and there was not one of those present whom he did not break down, except Socrates himself.

But he said: What are you doing, you astonishing men? It was for just this reason, more than any other, that I sent the women away, so that they would not strike such a false note. For I have heard that a man should die in reverent silence. Be quiet, and be strong.

When we heard that, we were ashamed, and held back our tears. He walked about, and when he said that his legs were growing heavy, he lay down on his back, for so the man had told him. And the man who had given him the poison took hold of him, and after a while examined his feet and his legs. Then he pressed his foot hard and asked if he felt it. He said no. And after that, his shins. And going upward in this way he showed us that he was growing cold and stiff. And he touched him again himself, and said that when it reached his heart, then he would be gone.

By now the cold had come almost to the region of his belly, when he uncovered his face — for he had covered it — and said, and these were the last words he spoke: Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius. Pay it, and do not neglect it.
It shall be done, said Crito. But see if you have anything else to say.
To this question he gave no further answer. After a little while he stirred, and the man uncovered him, and his eyes were fixed. When Crito saw it, he closed his mouth and his eyes.
That, Echecrates, was the end of our friend, a man who was, as we would say, the best of all those of his time whom we knew, and besides the wisest and the most just.

divergences.phrase: ἄξιον κινδυνεῦσαι οἰομένῳ οὕτως ἔχειν — καλὸς γὰρ ὁ κίνδυνος
divergences.older: he may venture to think, not improperly or unworthily, that something of the kind is true. The venture is a glorious one
divergences.lectio: worth the risk for one who thinks it is so — for the risk is a fine one
divergences.note: Socrates has just said that no man of sense would insist the story is exactly true. What he claims for it is narrower than Jowett's 'venture to think': believing it is a risk, the same word as the 'risk' of neglecting the soul at 107c, and the risk is worth running. The edition keeps 'risk' both times and the plain word 'fine'.

divergences.phrase: ὦ Κρίτων, τῷ Ἀσκληπιῷ ὀφείλομεν ἀλεκτρυόνα· ἀλλὰ ἀπόδοτε καὶ μὴ ἀμελήσητε
divergences.older: Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?
divergences.lectio: Crito, we owe a cock to Asclepius. Pay it, and do not neglect it.
divergences.note: The verbs are plural: 'we owe', and 'pay it' said to all of them. Jowett makes the debt Socrates' own and turns the command into a request. A cock was the offering made to the god of healing by someone cured; what Socrates means by it the Greek does not say, and the edition does not say either.

divergences.phrase: ἀνδρός, ὡς ἡμεῖς φαῖμεν ἄν, τῶν τότε ὧν ἐπειράθημεν ἀρίστου καὶ ἄλλως φρονιμωτάτου καὶ δικαιοτάτου
divergences.older: concerning whom I may truly say, that of all the men of his time whom I have known, he was the wisest and justest and best.
divergences.lectio: a man who was, as we would say, the best of all those of his time whom we knew, and besides the wisest and the most just.
divergences.note: Phaedo speaks for the whole circle ('we would say'), limits the claim to the men they had known, and puts 'best' first, with wisdom and justice added after it. Jowett changes 'we' to 'I', adds 'truly', and reorders the three words to end on 'best'. The edition keeps Plato's order and his restraint.

divergences.older: a man should die in peace
divergences.lectio: a man should die in reverent silence
divergences.note: Euphemia is the hush kept at a sacrifice, when nothing ill-omened may be said. Socrates is not asking for calm for his own sake; he is treating his death as a rite. 'In peace' loses that.
